source.version: arXiv:2510.26490v1 [cs.HC], 30 Oct 2025, as printed on PDF p. 1.

studies.label: Randomized persona-guided versus standard ChatGPT library-ideation experiment; setting not stated

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 4, section 4, first paragraph (randomization); PDF p. 5, section 5, first paragraph (analyzed conversation dataset)
counts_source.quote: A total of 105 undergraduate students [...] Random assignment allocated 73 participants to the treatment group and 32 to the control group. [...] The final dataset comprised 101 conversation logs

arms.name: Persona-guided ChatGPT (Taylor and Alex)
arms.description: Participants could freely switch within the same conversation between Taylor, prompted for divergent thinking with a higher temperature, and Alex, prompted for convergent thinking with a lower temperature. Both personas were available in the same randomized treatment arm (PDF p. 4, section 4; PDF p. 11, section 6).

arms.name: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
arms.description: The same interface and both persona buttons were available, but both buttons routed input to the identical baseline ChatGPT model, producing unmodified responses (PDF p. 4, section 4).

studies.task: Undergraduate students generated ideas for making libraries more attractive to young adults in a single timed chat session; ideas were extracted from their user transcripts (PDF p. 4, section 4; PDF p. 9, section 5.3).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT (participant-facing model/version not stated)
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 4, section 4, condition descriptions; GPT-4.1 and text-embedding-3-large on PDF p. 9, section 5.3, are analysis tools, not identified as the participant-facing chat model.

preregistration.where: No preregistration statement or registry link was found in the complete paper.

estimates.outcome: Between-participant portfolio distance to same-condition peers (paper primary originality measure)
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Ideas were extracted from user transcripts using GPT-4.1. OpenAI text-embedding-3-large provided normalized idea embeddings; each participant portfolio was represented by their mean-pooled centroid. For each participant, mean cosine distance from their portfolio centroid to same-condition peers; the reported arm means average these participant-level scores (PDF pp. 9-10, section 5.3).
estimates.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, section 5.3, paragraph beginning Same-condition originality
sources.quote: Same-condition originality showed the largest effect (Treatment M=0.34, Control M=0.28; Welch’s t, p=2.20 × 10−6), indicating that persona-guided teams occupied more distinct semantic positions.

estimates.notes: The paper calls this participant-level originality, but it compares different people’s portfolios and is coded diversity/across_people. Higher cosine distance means greater semantic separation. The measure is computed once per participant from other participants’ portfolios, rather than analyzed as independent idea pairs. Figure 6 labels the comparisons as Welch tests; the paper does not report their test statistics or degrees of freedom. No adjustment for dependence induced by shared reference portfolios is described. Numerical SDs, SEs and confidence-interval endpoints are not printed; the figure’s error-bar definition is not given and no values were read from bar heights or error bars. Analysis-specific participant counts are left null: section 5 gives the overall conversation dataset, and its arm split conflicts with Figure 6. Values available only in Figure 6 are not entered as statistics or counts. Figure 6 explicitly labels the same-condition measure primary; this is a paper designation, not evidence of preregistration. The source quote preserves the printed scientific notation for the p-value.

estimates.outcome: Between-participant portfolio distance to all participants
estimates.question: across_people

For each participant, mean cosine distance from their portfolio centroid to all participants; whether the all-participant reference set excludes the participant themself is not specified (PDF pp. 9-10, section 5.3).
estimates.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)

estimates.outcome: Between-participant portfolio distance to nearest cross-condition neighbor
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Ideas were extracted from user transcripts using GPT-4.1. OpenAI text-embedding-3-large provided normalized idea embeddings; each participant portfolio was represented by their mean-pooled centroid. For each participant, cosine distance to the nearest participant portfolio centroid in the opposite condition; arm means summarize participant-level nearest-neighbor distances (PDF pp. 9-10, section 5.3).
estimates.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, section 5.3, paragraph beginning Same-condition originality, cross-condition nearest-neighbor result
sources.quote: nearest neighbor distances confirmed greater between-condition separation (Treatment M=0.20, Control M=0.17; p<.01).

estimates.notes: The paper calls this participant-level originality, but it compares different people’s portfolios and is coded diversity/across_people. Higher cosine distance means greater semantic separation. The measure is computed once per participant from other participants’ portfolios, rather than analyzed as independent idea pairs. Figure 6 labels the comparisons as Welch tests; the paper does not report their test statistics or degrees of freedom. No adjustment for dependence induced by shared reference portfolios is described. Numerical SDs, SEs and confidence-interval endpoints are not printed; the figure’s error-bar definition is not given and no values were read from bar heights or error bars. Analysis-specific participant counts are left null: section 5 gives the overall conversation dataset, and its arm split conflicts with Figure 6. Values available only in Figure 6 are not entered as statistics or counts. This is an alternative reference-set definition of S1-O1. It measures distance to the opposite condition, not dispersion within the participant’s own condition. estimates.outcome: Idea fluency (number of ideas per participant)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Number of ideas extracted from each participant’s user transcript. A two-stage content-analysis pipeline used GPT-4.1 for structured idea extraction, then category induction to organize ideas into thematic groups; the fluency outcome is the idea count, not the category count (PDF p. 9, section 5.3).
estimates.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)

sources.locator: PDF p. 9, section 5.3, paragraph beginning Idea fluency
sources.quote: Idea fluency showed no significant between-condition differences, though control participants generated slightly more ideas on average (Treatment M=8.55, SD=3.85; Control M=9.23, SD=3.37).

estimates.notes: The paper states that the between-condition difference was not significant but prints no fluency p-value, test statistic, SE, interval or standardized effect. The SDs describe the participant-level idea counts, which is the basis for se_basis=participant; no contrast SE has been supplied or computed. Fluency-specific participant counts are not printed. All estimate-level counts remain null rather than borrowing either inconsistent arm split from the overall results text or the originality figure. The study-level analyzed total is retained separately. No raw difference or standardized effect is calculated.

estimates.outcome: Within-participant idea-portfolio variation (mean pairwise semantic distance)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Mean pairwise semantic distance among ideas within each participant’s own portfolio; the semantic-analysis pipeline uses OpenAI text-embedding-3-large. The two condition means summarize within-participant portfolio variation (PDF pp. 9-10, section 5.3).
estimates.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)

sources.locator: PDF p. 10, section 5.3, paragraph beginning Within-participant idea diversity
sources.quote: Within-participant idea diversity showed no group differences (mean pairwise distance: Treatment M=0.59, Control M=0.59, p=.90), suggesting that originality gains resulted from between-participant differentiation rather than increased internal portfolio variation.

estimates.notes: The paper calls this within-participant idea diversity; it is coded flexibility because the variation is among one person’s ideas. Higher scores indicate greater internal semantic variation and thus greater flexibility. The comparison is between independently randomized people, not a paired-condition design. The paper prints a p-value but gives no test name specifically for this outcome, test statistic, degrees of freedom, SD, SE or confidence interval. The stated measure is a within-participant portfolio summary, so se_basis is participant. Outcome-specific analyzed counts, including any exclusion of portfolios with too few ideas, are not printed; no overall sample count or conflicting arm split has been assumed for this analysis. The source quote preserves the p-value’s printed precision.

open_items: The individual randomization is explicit, but the paper does not identify laboratory supervision, online-panel delivery, or ordinary-work/coursework delivery. No permitted design_class subtype can be confirmed; design_class is null rather than inventing the RCT setting (PDF pp. 4-5, section 4; reconciled screening also leaves the subtype unresolved). The participant institution and study country are not identified.

Confirm the analyzed arm allocation. The results text states 69 persona and 32 control conversation logs, while the arm labels in Figure 6 disagree. Study-level n_analyzed=101 is explicitly printed, but arm-level analyzed counts remain null; figure-only counts are not transcribed into estimate fields (PDF p. 5, section 5; PDF p. 10, Figure 6).

The output-specific participant counts for fluency and within-participant portfolio variation are not printed, and the originality figure conflicts with the results-text allocation. Estimate-level n_total, n_treatment and n_control remain null until analysis-specific inclusion counts are confirmed (PDF pp. 9-10, section 5.3).

The paper states four exclusions but lists reason counts of 1, 2, 1 and 1 without stating whether reasons overlap. The separately stated survey exclusions are not applied to the conversation-output dataset (PDF p. 5, section 5, continuing on PDF p. 6).

The participant-facing ChatGPT model/version and its release year, as well as complete persona prompts, are not stated. GPT-4.1 is named for post hoc idea extraction only, and the embedding model for scoring; neither establishes the chat model used by participants (PDF p. 4, section 4; PDF p. 9, section 5.3).

For the portfolio-distance measures, the paper does not print arm SDs, SEs, numerical confidence-interval bounds, test statistics or degrees of freedom. Figure 6 does not define its error bars, and no plotted values are estimated (PDF p. 10, section 5.3 and Figure 6). Fluency lacks a printed p-value or numerical inferential statistic (PDF p. 9, section 5.3).

The reference-set implementation is incomplete: self-exclusion in the all-participant distance and the treatment of dependence from shared comparison portfolios are not specified (PDF pp. 9-10, section 5.3).

The excluded question-asking analysis prints control counts exceeding the randomized control arm. Its observational unit is not established and those process-analysis counts must not be used for creative-output estimates (PDF p. 8, section 5.2; PDF p. 4, section 4).
notes: Extraction date: 2026-10-11. The complete markdown conversion was read sequentially, including the full references; the PDF contains no appendix or identified supplement. Every cited substantive PDF page was checked using pymupdf text extraction; Figure 6 was also inspected directly in memory. PDF page numbers match the printed page numbers. This is one individually randomized experiment comparing two generative-AI configurations. Taylor and Alex are available within one treatment arm and are not independently randomized arms. The setting cannot be confirmed, so design_class is deliberately null; this does not imply that random assignment was absent. All eligible outputs were produced with AI available in the same session; no unassisted follow-up was conducted. The three reference-set variants of screening outcome S1-O1 are retained as separate estimate records. No estimate combines arms, derives an effect, converts a p-value, or imputes a count. Figure-only numerical information is not entered. Country and the participant-facing model year are not inferred from author affiliations or the paper date. No shared sample is identified in the reconciled form. Only the designated extraction file was written.
